title: Steve Bannon Convicted of Contempt of Congress for Defying Jan. 6 Subpoena
description_short: A jury convicted Steve Bannon in 2022 of two contempt-of-Congress counts for refusing to testify and produce documents subpoenaed by the House January 6 committee.
description_medium: The Justice Department reports that a federal jury found Steve Bannon guilty on July 22, 2022, of two contempt-of-Congress counts: refusing to appear for a deposition and refusing to produce documents subpoenaed by the House January 6 committee. The court later sentenced him to four months in prison. The supplied New York Times link concerns Donald Trump’s indictment and does not support Bannon’s case. No claim about a later pardon is made here because the cited source packet does not substantiate one.
description_long: A federal jury found Steve Bannon guilty on July 22, 2022, of two counts of contempt of Congress after he refused to appear for a deposition and refused to produce documents in response to a subpoena from the House Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the United States Capitol. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia describes the verdict and the two refusals in its public sentencing announcement. The court imposed a four-month prison sentence. These facts support an entry about the subpoena, conviction, and sentence. The New York Times article supplied with this record is about Donald Trump’s January 6 indictment; it does not document Bannon’s subpoena case, verdict, or sentence. The packet also mentions a later pardon, but the linked source does not support that separate action, so it is omitted pending a Bannon-specific clemency record. The conviction and sentencing should be stated as court outcomes, without conflating Bannon’s conduct with Trump’s indictment or inferring why clemency may or may not have been granted.

title: Yosemite Ranger Shannon Joslin Fired After Hanging Transgender Pride Flag
description_short: AP reports Yosemite ranger Shannon “SJ” Joslin was fired after hanging a transgender pride flag; this single case does not establish a broader pattern.
description_medium: The AP reports that Yosemite ranger and biologist Shannon “SJ” Joslin was fired after helping hang a large transgender pride flag on El Capitan in May 2025. The termination letter cited unacceptable conduct and the flag incident; Joslin said the display was in a personal capacity. The article documents one case, not a pattern across federal agencies.
description_long: The Associated Press reports that Yosemite National Park ranger and biologist Shannon “SJ” Joslin was fired after hanging a large transgender pride flag on El Capitan in May 2025. AP says Joslin and other climbers displayed the flag for about two hours and removed it voluntarily. A termination letter cited failure to demonstrate acceptable conduct in Joslin’s role as a biologist and referred to the May incident; Joslin said the action was taken as a private citizen. The article also reports that other Yosemite employees were placed on administrative leave while the park investigated. These details support a focused account of Joslin’s firing and the stated basis in the termination letter, with the employee’s characterization separately attributed. The article does not establish that federal agencies broadly fired transgender employees or workers who supported trans rights, nor does it document the additional examples in the broader original title. Narrowing the title to the AP-documented Yosemite case keeps the entry within the evidence. Any broader pattern would require separate agency records and case-specific reporting.

title: Bolton Reorganizes NSC Global Health Security Unit
description_short: Bolton’s 2018 NSC reorganization eliminated a standalone global health directorate; reporting said related duties remained elsewhere.
description_medium: Contemporaneous reporting says John Bolton’s 2018 NSC reorganization eliminated its standalone Global Health Security directorate. The Los Angeles Times attributed the decision to Bolton; TIME quoted an administration official saying related responsibilities were absorbed elsewhere. This supports a reorganization, but not the claim that all preparedness functions ended or a specific operational harm occurred.
description_long: In 2018, National Security Adviser John Bolton reorganized the National Security Council, eliminating its standalone Global Health Security directorate. The Los Angeles Times’ later account of the pandemic response attributes the decision to Bolton. TIME’s contemporaneous reporting says the team was disbanded as part of a broader NSC restructuring and quotes an administration official saying related responsibilities were absorbed into another directorate. The available sources therefore support describing the loss of a dedicated global-health office and a change in organizational structure. title: Trump Removes State Department Inspector General Steve Linick
description_short: Trump removed State Department IG Steve Linick in May 2020 amid inquiries involving Mike Pompeo; motive remains disputed.
description_medium: Congressional statements and a subsequent inquiry confirm Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick in May 2020. Linick’s office had inquiries involving Secretary Mike Pompeo. Lawmakers alleged retaliation; Pompeo denied knowing about one inquiry, and the administration cited lack of confidence. The supplied USA Today link is an unrelated wildfire story and cannot support this entry.
description_long: President Donald Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick in May 2020. The congressional record and the congressional inquiry into the removal document that Linick’s office had several open matters involving Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, including review of the emergency arms-sale process and a separate inquiry concerning use of department staff for personal tasks. Lawmakers said they were investigating whether the dismissal was retaliatory. That allegation must remain attributed: the existence of pending inquiries and the timing of the removal do not by themselves prove motive. Pompeo said he recommended Linick’s removal and denied knowing about one investigation; the White House’s notification cited the president’s lack of confidence. title: Trump Commutes Michael H. Ashley’s Prison Sentence on January 19, 2021
description_short: Trump commuted Michael H. Ashley’s prison sentence to time served, or zero days if he had served none, on January 19, 2021.
description_medium: The Justice Department roster lists Michael H. Ashley’s January 19, 2021 commutation and the original 36-month prison term, five years of supervised release, and $49,307,759.84 in restitution. The signed clemency warrant says Trump commuted the prison sentence to time served, or to zero days if Ashley had served no time. The warrant text does not say that supervised release or restitution was forgiven, and no recipient-specific rationale is given.
description_long: The Justice Department’s commutations roster lists Michael H. Ashley under January 19, 2021, in connection with a 2019 Eastern District of New York bank-fraud case. The roster records the original sentence as 36 months in prison, five years of supervised release, and $49,307,759.84 in restitution. The signed clemency warrant supplies the term missing from the public roster: President Trump commuted Ashley’s prison sentence to time already served, or to zero days’ imprisonment if no time had been served. This establishes a reduction of the custodial term. The warrant language available here does not state that supervised release or restitution was also commuted or forgiven, so those terms should not be described as changed. The documents also give no recipient-specific reason for the decision. The entry should describe the narrow, documented effect of the commutation and avoid inferring a corrupt motive from the grant itself. The original “Corrupt Pardons” categorization is not established by the clemency documents and should be reviewed separately.
